title: Mahakassapa comes
hook: the great ascetic comes to him (Buddhacarita 17)

segments.voice: Yesterday: many come, friends, fire-keepers and a king, and your line, everything is burning. Today one more arrives, a man who had already given up nearly everything.

Two robes on a roadside. One is a patched outer robe, but soft, folded into a seat under a tree. The other is rough hemp, worn thin, stitched together from rags. In a little while, the two men wearing them will swap. The man with the soft robe is a seeker who has already left a wealthy home. The man with the rags is the Buddha. This is how the discourses remember the meeting with Kassapa, later called Mahakassapa, great Kassapa. And the poem, in its seventeenth canto, sends him walking toward the Buddha too.
screen: `TWO ROBES ON A ROADSIDE.` → `ONE SOFT, ONE RAGGED.` → `KASSAPA IS COMING.`

segments.voice: First, what he left. Tradition remembers Kassapa as born into a wealthy brahmin family, and leaving it all, house, riches, a wife, to go looking for freedom. Later tradition adds a tender detail: his wife, Bhadda, wanted the same thing, and the two of them went forth together, parting at a crossroads to walk different roads. Second, the meeting. In his own words in the discourses, Kassapa says he saw the Buddha sitting by a shrine on the road between Rajagaha and Nalanda, and knew at once: this is my teacher. He bowed and said so, and the Buddha taught him there by the road. Third, the robes. Kassapa folded his cloak for the Buddha to sit on. The Buddha remarked how soft it was. Kassapa offered it, and the Buddha gave him his own worn rag-robe in return. It's a small, strange exchange, and some readers take it as a sign: the teacher handing his robe to someone who would carry the teaching on. Fourth, what he became. The discourses list Kassapa as foremost among the monks who kept the strict ascetic practices: living in the forest, eating only alms food, wearing rag-robes. He came after the first five, after Yasas and the fire-keepers. He wasn't the first. But in the stories, he became one of the great ones, and tradition says that after the Buddha's death it was Kassapa who called the monks together to remember what had been taught. The great ones don't all arrive at the start.
screen: `A WEALTHY HOME, LEFT BEHIND.` · `THIS IS MY TEACHER.` · `A SOFT CLOAK FOR A RAG-ROBE.` · `FOREMOST IN THE STRICT PRACTICES.` · then, large: `THE GREAT ONES ARRIVE.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind someone who joined something after you did, a family, a team, a circle of friends, and who may never have felt part of the founding story. Notice one thing they carry now that no one else does, and rest with the breath, holding them in that light.
Mahakassapa comes. A wealthy brahmin who left home, met the Buddha by a roadside shrine, and traded his soft cloak for a rag-robe. Today's word.
Your line: the great ones arrive. Coming late made him no less great. That's day seven hundred twenty.

screen: `DAY 720 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: THE REST OF THE POEM.`

howItsDone: Mahakassapa is honored in Theravada as a model of forest and ascetic practice, and in Zen lineages as the first heir of the teaching after the Buddha. Monks in forest traditions still keep some of the strict practices he is remembered for.

fork.setup: you're Kassapa. you've folded your good cloak for the teacher to sit on, and he says how soft it is. what do you do?
fork.reveal: Kassapa offers it, and the Buddha gives him his own worn rag-robe in return.

trapdoor: what you thought: the great disciples were all there at the start.
what it means: Kassapa came later, after the first five and the fire-keepers, and still became one of the great ones.
what a scholar hears: in the discourses Kassapa tells the meeting himself, ending with the robe exchange (SN 16.11).

chat.says: Why do people say the Buddha gave Kassapa his robe?
options: By a roadside shrine they swapped: Kassapa's soft cloak for the Buddha's rag-robe.
Kassapa was one of the five who first heard him, so he got the robe.
Kassapa asked for it as payment for leaving his wealthy home.
chat.meaning: In the discourses, Kassapa folded his soft cloak as a seat; the Buddha remarked on it, took it, and gave his worn rag-robe in return.

Mahakassapa.meaning: great Kassapa, foremost in the strict ascetic practices

Bhadda.meaning: Kassapa's wife, who also went forth, says later tradition

Rajagaha.meaning: a city ringed by hills, Bimbisara's capital

Nalanda.meaning: a town on the road from Rajagaha

brahmin.meaning: a member of the priestly class

sources.ref: Buddhacarita 17 (the going forth of great disciples, including Kashyapa)
Samyutta Nikaya 16.11 (Civara Sutta: the meeting at the Bahuputta shrine and the exchange of robes)
Anguttara Nikaya 1 (Etadagga Vagga: foremost in the ascetic practices)
Samyutta Nikaya 16.5 (Jinna Sutta: Kassapa as forest dweller, alms-food eater and rag-robe wearer)

notes: Canto 17 survives in Tibetan and Chinese, not in Ashvaghosha's Sanskrit; confirm that it tells Kashyapa's going forth and that he is described as a wealthy brahmin who left a wife. The canto also tells of other great disciples (Shariputra, Maudgalyayana) whose story the path begins on day 725; the script leaves them out on purpose.
Bhadda Kapilani and the parting at the crossroads come from the commentaries (Theragatha/Therigatha commentary); framed as 'later tradition'.

SN 16.11: confirm the Bahuputta shrine between Rajagaha and Nalanda, Kassapa recognizing his teacher, folding his outer robe as a seat, the Buddha remarking its softness, and the exchange for the Buddha's hempen rag-robes.
'Buddhists have long read it as a sign' of succession: soften to 'some readers' if a reviewer prefers.
First council led by Kassapa: Vinaya Cullavagga 11; framed as 'tradition says'.
howItsDone: Zen lineages name Mahakashyapa as the first patriarch after the Buddha; confirm wording.

Editor: Kassapa's wealthy brahmin birth and wife now framed as 'tradition remembers' (not confirmed in canto 17); 'Buddhists have long read it' softened to 'some readers'; added SN 16.5 for the forest, alms food and rag-robe practices named in the teach; howItsDone no longer says 'across Buddhist traditions'.

Audit: in SN 16.11 Kassapa's outer robe is itself made of patches (patapilotika sanghati), soft to the touch, and the Buddha's are hempen rag-robes; the hook no longer calls Kassapa's 'a good cloak' against plain rags.
